items.prose: A fair die is rolled. You learn the result is even.
items.question: What is the chance it is a 6?

options.why: You kept all six faces as the denominator. Only 2, 4 and 6 are left.
You treated 6 and not 6 as equally likely. Three faces are left and one is a 6.

feedback.correct: Three faces are left, and one of them is a 6.
feedback.generic: Count the faces that agree with the news, then the 6s among them.

explain.text: Even leaves 2, 4 and 6, three equally likely faces. One of them is a 6, so the chance is $\tfrac{1}{3}$.

items.prose: A red die and a blue die are rolled. You learn the red die shows 4.
items.question: What is the chance the blue die shows 6?

options.why: You found the chance of red 4 and blue 6 together. The red 4 is already known.
You took the 4 away from the blue die. The dice are separate, so all six blue faces remain.

feedback.correct: The news is about the other die, so the chance does not move.
feedback.generic: Ask which outcomes the news rules out, and whether any of them involve the blue die.

explain.text: Learning the red die keeps row 4 of the table: six cells, one for each blue face. One of the six has a blue 6, so the chance stays at $\tfrac{1}{6}$.

items.prose: Three fair coins are tossed. You learn that at least two of them landed heads.
items.question: What is the chance all three are heads? Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.correct: Four outcomes are left, and one of them is all heads.
feedback.generic: List the outcomes with at least two heads, then count the ones with three.

byKey.whole: You divided by all 8 outcomes. The news leaves only 4 of them.
byKey.third-coin: You treated the news as two named coins landing heads. It says at least two, so HTH and THH count too.

explain.text: At least two heads leaves HHT, HTH, THH and HHH. Only HHH has three heads, so the chance is $\tfrac{1}{4}$.

items.prose: Two cards are dealt from a standard 52-card deck without replacement. The first card is a king.
items.question: What is the chance the second card is also a king? Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.correct: Three kings are left among 51 cards.
feedback.generic: Count what is left in the deck after the first card has gone.

byKey.replaced: You used 4 kings in 52 cards, as if the first card went back.
byKey.deck: You took a king away but kept 52 cards. The deck is down to 51.

explain.text: After one king is dealt, 51 cards remain and 3 of them are kings. The chance is $\tfrac{3}{51} = \tfrac{1}{17} \approx 0.0588$.

items.prose: Two fair dice are rolled. You learn the total is 9. The shaded cells are the outcomes that are left.
items.question: What is the chance the first die shows an even number?

options.why: You divided by all 36 cells. Only the four shaded cells are left.
You counted one even first die. Both (4, 5) and (6, 3) start with an even number.

feedback.correct: Two of the four shaded cells start with an even number.
feedback.generic: Work inside the shaded cells only.

explain.text: A total of 9 leaves (3, 6), (4, 5), (5, 4) and (6, 3). Two of them start with an even number, so the chance is $\tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac{1}{2}$.

items.prose: A bag holds 5 red and 3 blue counters. Two are drawn, one after the other, without replacement.
items.question: What is the chance both are red? Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.correct: The second factor is conditional on the first red having gone.
feedback.generic: Multiply the chance of a first red by the chance of a second red given the first.

byKey.replaced: You multiplied $\tfrac{5}{8}$ by itself, as if the counter went back.
byKey.same-bag: You took a red away but kept 8 counters in the bag. Seven are left.

explain.text: The multiplication rule gives $\tfrac{5}{8} \cdot \tfrac{4}{7} = \tfrac{20}{56} = \tfrac{5}{14}$. The second factor counts 4 reds among the 7 counters left.

items.prose: A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two are drawn without replacement. The tree shows every branch.
items.question: What is the chance the second counter is blue? Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.correct: Two paths end in a blue second counter, and their chances add.
feedback.generic: Find every path that ends in blue, multiply along each, then add.

byKey.one-path: You used only red then blue. Blue then blue also ends in a blue second counter.
byKey.blue-blue: You used only blue then blue. Red then blue also ends in a blue second counter.

explain.text: Red then blue gives $\tfrac{3}{5} \cdot \tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac{3}{10}$, and blue then blue gives $\tfrac{2}{5} \cdot \tfrac{1}{4} = \tfrac{1}{10}$. They add to $\tfrac{2}{5}$, the same as the first draw.

items.prose: A trading signal fires on 30% of trending days and 10% of other days. The market trends on 40% of days.
items.question: On a day picked at random, what is the chance the signal fires? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: Two routes lead to a signal, weighted by how often each kind of day occurs.
feedback.generic: Split the days into trending and not trending, then add the two routes.

byKey.average: You averaged 30% and 10% equally. Trending days are only 40% of days, so weight them.
byKey.trend-only: You counted only trending days. The signal also fires on 10% of the other days.

explain.text: Trending and firing has chance $0.4 \times 0.3 = 0.12$. Not trending and firing has $0.6 \times 0.1 = 0.06$. The routes add to $0.18$.
